headline: Colby Wants Europe to Lead
deck: Washington’s Europe posture review is being built to shift conventional defense onto European allies. Reuters says an internal Terms of Reference sets September and November decision clocks and at least four force options.
body: Elbridge Colby told NATO’s North Atlantic Council in Brussels on 27 August that Washington is already conducting its Europe Posture Review, with analysis running through U.S. European Command and SHAPE [E1]. He said the review will “encourage, enable, and impel” a transition toward a more durable European-led conventional defense [E2]. That language makes burden transfer the review’s stated strategic purpose, even before any basing decision is taken [E1][E2]. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte publicly framed the visit as part of consultations over the “best footprint” for U.S. forces in Europe [E8].

Colby’s speech places the review inside his “NATO 3.0” thesis: European allies take primary responsibility for conventional defense while U.S. forces remain available for wider global priorities [E2]. He explicitly named the Western Hemisphere and the First Island Chain as U.S. priorities, while calling Europe critical and NATO central to Atlantic security [E1]. The inference is that Washington is designing a European posture that can carry more of the continent’s conventional load while preserving American freedom to shift forces elsewhere [E1][E2]. Europe’s military buildup is therefore being treated as an input to U.S. posture choices as well as an allied spending commitment [E1].

Reuters says the internal Terms of Reference requires at least four force-posture options for Secretary Pete Hegseth by 6 November [E5]. The options are to cover force numbers, locations, pace of adjustment and costs, according to the document Reuters reviewed [E7]. The same document calls for EUCOM’s commander to join a decision briefing with Colby by 18 September [E6]. Those dates turn a broad strategic review into a staged decision process with a September narrowing point and a November options package [E5][E6].

War.gov published Colby’s remarks and described the Terms of Reference as distributed to allied capitals; it did not publish the TOR text alongside the speech [E3]. The four-option structure and the 18 September and 6 November deadlines therefore remain Reuters-document reporting [E5][E6]. Colby said the review has “no preconceived fixed goal or outcome,” and no withdrawal order or public troop-reduction target appears in his remarks [E4]. The official record establishes the strategic direction and consultation process, while the exact menu going to Hegseth remains inside the unpublished TOR [E3][E4][E5].

The roughly 80,000 U.S. forces now in Europe provide the scale against which allies are reading the review, Reuters reported [E5]. Neither Colby’s remarks nor the public NATO exchange sets a replacement force level [E4][E8]. Colby instead described a posture shaped by warfighting readiness, allied capacity, U.S. global demands, access, basing and overflight [E1]. A review built on those variables can produce reductions, relocations or a different force mix without making any one outcome inevitable [E4][E7].

For European capitals, pressure now lands on capability: Colby said allies must assume primary responsibility for conventional defense and can lead support for Ukraine’s self-defense [E1][E2]. Rutte answered by pointing to stronger European and Canadian contributions and said consultations over the U.S. footprint were already happening [E8]. If Washington seeks a smaller or more globally flexible American posture, European armies will have to cover more of the conventional defense plan on a timetable compatible with U.S. global force demands [E1][E2]. The posture review is where that political demand acquires basing, cost and readiness consequences [E7].

The sharpest signal on 27 August was Colby’s choice of verbs. Washington intends to “encourage, enable, and impel” the transition, language that makes the posture review an instrument for changing who carries Europe’s conventional defense [E2]. Hegseth has yet to choose from the force options Reuters says are due on 6 November [E5]. The Pentagon has already set the vector: European-led conventional defense, with the American footprint redesigned around it [E2][E4].
